questions.question: For the list [5,6,7], what does xs bind to when matched against the pattern (x:xs)?
options: 6, the second element
[6,7], the rest of the list after the head
[5,6,7], the whole original list
7, the last element
questions.explanation: x binds to the head, 5. xs binds to everything else, as a list: [6,7]. It is not the second element on its own — it is the entire remaining tail, however many elements that turns out to be.
optionFeedback: 6 is the head of xs, not xs itself — xs is the whole tail [6,7], not one element plucked out of it.
Correct — xs is the entire remainder of the list once the head is removed, still wrapped up as a list.
That would mean nothing was removed at all; x is bound to 5 specifically so it is peeled off, leaving xs as the shorter list [6,7].
7 is the last element of xs, but xs itself is the pair [6,7], not a single element.

questions.question: describeList [42] prints "x = 42, xs = []". What does this show about xs for a one-element list?
options: That matching a singleton against (x:xs) fails, since there's nothing left for xs
That xs is bound to the empty list [] — a valid, ordinary value, not an error and not "no value"
That xs is bound to 42 as well, duplicating x
That describeList must have a bug, since xs should never be empty
questions.explanation: (x:xs) matches any list with at least one element. For [42], removing the head 42 leaves exactly []: a real, valid list value of length zero, not a failure and not the absence of a value. This is precisely why every list recursion still needs its own [] equation — the [] a singleton produces has to go somewhere on the next call.
optionFeedback: The match succeeds fine — [42] has a head (42) and a tail ([]), which is exactly what (x:xs) requires: at least one element.
Correct — [] is an ordinary, valid list value here, exactly the same [] you would pass in directly.
x and xs are bound independently to different parts of the list; xs is not a copy of x, it is what remains after x is removed.
This is the correct, expected behaviour for a singleton — not a bug. A one-element list's tail is always [].

questions.question: Why are [] and (x:xs) an exhaustive pair of patterns for any list?
options: Because every Haskell list has either zero or exactly one element
Because every list is, by construction, either empty or an element consed onto some other list — there is no third case
Because Haskell forbids lists longer than two elements without recursion
Because (x:xs) only matches lists of even length
questions.explanation: The previous lesson showed every list is built by consing, all the way down to []. So a list is either [] (zero cons cells) or some x : rest (at least one cons cell) — there is no other shape a list can take.
optionFeedback: Lists can have any length — three, ten, a million elements — and (x:xs) still matches all of them, since xs can itself be arbitrarily long.
Correct — the cons-cell structure guarantees every list is one of exactly these two shapes.
There's no length restriction of this kind; (x:xs) matches a list of any length ≥ 1, with xs absorbing everything after the head.
(x:xs) matches any non-empty list regardless of length or parity — it says nothing about how many elements remain in xs.

questions.question: A function is missing its [] equation. What happens when GHC compiles it?
options: GHC refuses to compile, reporting a missing pattern error
GHC compiles it successfully; the gap surfaces only if [] is passed in at run time
GHC automatically inserts a default [] case
The function silently returns [] whenever it is called
questions.explanation: Missing patterns are (at most) a warning, not a compile error. GHC's type checker verifies the equations that exist are well-typed — it doesn't prove every possible input is handled. The gap only becomes visible as a Non-exhaustive patterns crash when [] actually reaches the function.
optionFeedback: A missing pattern is not a type error, so it does not block compilation — this is exactly what makes it a dangerous mistake to skip.
Correct — the program compiles fine; the missing case only bites once an empty list is actually passed in.
GHC never invents a case on your behalf; an uncovered pattern stays uncovered until you write it.
Without a [] equation, calling the function on [] crashes — it does not fall back to returning [] automatically.

questions.question: Why is sum' [] = 0 the right base case, rather than, say, sum' [] = 1?
options: 0 is simply the smallest Integer, so it's the conventional default
0 is the identity for addition: adding it to any total leaves that total unchanged, matching what summing 'nothing more' should do
Because the type signature requires the base case to be 0
It doesn't matter which value is used, as long as it's a constant
questions.explanation: sum' [5] must equal 5 + sum' [] = 5 + 0 = 5. Any base value other than 0 would silently shift every result — sum' [5] with base 1 would wrongly give 6. The base case has to be the identity element for whatever operation combines the elements.
optionFeedback: Integer has no smallest value at all (it's unbounded below) — that's not why 0 was chosen here.
Correct — 0 is addition's identity, so appending it to a running total never changes that total.
The signature sum' :: [Integer] -> Integer only fixes the type of the result, not its value for the empty case.
It matters a great deal — a wrong base case silently offsets every single result by a constant amount.

questions.question: In length' (_:xs) = 1 + length' xs, why is the head matched with _ instead of a name like x?
options: Because Haskell requires wildcards in every recursive pattern
Because the head's value never appears on the right-hand side — length' only needs to know that an element exists, not what it is
Because _ makes the function run faster
Because x is a reserved keyword in Haskell
questions.explanation: length' counts elements; it never inspects what any element actually is. Naming it x would be misleading, since x is then unused. _ documents, right in the pattern, that the value is irrelevant here.
optionFeedback: Plenty of recursive patterns in this lesson name the head explicitly, e.g. sum' (x:xs) = x + sum' xs — wildcards are used only when the value truly isn't needed.
Correct — _ signals 'this value doesn't matter', which is exactly length''s situation.
_ and a named variable compile to the same underlying pattern match; there's no performance difference.
x is an ordinary identifier in Haskell, not a keyword — it could be used here, it's just unnecessary.

questions.question: In doubleAll (x:xs) = (x * 2) : doubleAll xs, what would happen if : were replaced with ++?
options: Nothing — : and ++ are interchangeable for lists
A type error, because ++ needs a list on both sides, and (x * 2) is a single Integer, not a list
It would still work, but run twice as slowly
It would double every element twice instead of once
questions.explanation: ++ :: [a] -> [a] -> [a] requires both operands to already be lists. (x * 2) is a bare Integer. To use ++ here you would need [x * 2] ++ doubleAll xs — wrapping it in a singleton list first.
optionFeedback: : takes an element and a list; ++ takes two lists. They require different-shaped arguments and are not drop-in replacements.
Correct — (x * 2) :: Integer is not a list, so ++ rejects it as a type mismatch.
The issue isn't speed, it's that the expression wouldn't compile at all as written.
Swapping the operator doesn't change how many times doubling happens — it changes how the result is joined, if it compiled at all.

questions.question: What does doubleAll [] evaluate to, and why?
options: An error, since there's nothing to double
[], because doubling every element of an empty list still produces an empty list
[0], since doubling nothing gives zero
It never terminates
questions.explanation: The base case doubleAll [] = [] says exactly this: transforming zero elements yields zero elements. There's no arithmetic to perform, so no error and no placeholder value — just the empty list, unchanged.
optionFeedback: doubleAll is total: it has a defined answer for every list, including the empty one — no error is thrown.
Correct — the base case matches [] directly and returns [] with no further work.
There's no element to double in an empty list, so no 0 is manufactured — the result is simply empty, not a list containing a zero.
The base case is checked first and matches immediately; there's no recursive call at all for [], so it terminates instantly.

questions.question: In largerY, both branches of the guard recurse on xs. Why does the function still terminate?
options: It doesn't always terminate — it depends on the input
Because xs is one element shorter than the original list regardless of which branch runs, so the list still shrinks toward [] every single call
Because y decreases on every call
Because largerY has a hidden counter that limits recursion depth
questions.explanation: Whether the head is kept (x : largerY xs y) or dropped (largerY xs y), the recursive call is always on xs — the tail. Every call therefore processes a strictly shorter list than the one before it, guaranteeing the base case [] is eventually reached.
optionFeedback: It terminates for every finite input list — the shrinking happens unconditionally in both guard branches.
Correct — both branches recurse on xs, so the list shrinks by one element every call no matter which branch is taken.
y is passed through unchanged in both branches — largerY xs y keeps the same y, it's x and xs that shrink.
There's no counter; termination comes entirely from the list argument getting structurally smaller each call.

questions.question: What does positiveNumbers [-1,5,-3,8] return, and in what order?
options: [8,5], reversed from the input
[5,8], the positive elements, in their original relative order
[-1,-3], the elements that were dropped
[5,-3,8], skipping only the first element
questions.explanation: The recursion walks the list left to right and conses each surviving element onto the front of the (already-processed) rest, which preserves the original order: 5 comes before 8 in the input, and stays before it in the output.
optionFeedback: positiveNumbers doesn't reverse anything — consing here preserves order because the recursive call processes the tail first, in the same left-to-right sequence as the input.
Correct — -1 and -3 fail the x > 0 test and are skipped; 5 and 8 pass, in their original order.
That would be the complement of what positiveNumbers keeps — this lists the discarded elements, not the kept ones.
Every failing element is skipped, not just the first — both -1 and -3 are dropped from the result.

questions.question: Why does isSorted need three equations — [], [_], and (x:y:rest) — instead of the usual two?
options: Because Haskell requires exactly three equations for every recursive function
Because a one-element list is trivially sorted but doesn't match (x:y:rest), which needs at least two elements
Because isSorted is defined for lists of at most three elements
It's a style choice; two equations would work identically
questions.explanation: (x:y:rest) requires at least two elements to match. A singleton list [5] is sorted by definition (nothing to compare it against) but has no second element, so it needs its own equation, [_] = True, separate from the [] base case.
optionFeedback: There's no fixed equation count in Haskell — most functions in this lesson use exactly two. isSorted specifically needs a third because of what (x:y:rest) can and can't match.
Correct — a singleton doesn't have a 'next element' to compare, so it needs its own True case, distinct from both [] and a genuine two-or-more-element list.
isSorted handles lists of any length — the recursive call (isSorted (y:rest)) keeps working through longer lists.
Without the [_] equation, calling isSorted [5] would fall through to (x:y:rest), fail to match (there's no y), and crash with Non-exhaustive patterns — it is not optional.

questions.question: Why is the recursive call isSorted (y:rest), and not isSorted rest?
options: isSorted rest would also work; (y:rest) is just a stylistic preference
Because y still needs to be compared against the element that follows it, so it must remain in the list passed to the next call
Because rest alone is not a valid list
To make the function run in constant time
questions.explanation: Each call only compares the current head against the next element. Dropping y and recursing on rest would skip the comparison between y and whatever comes after it — isSorted [5,1,9] would wrongly ignore whether 1 >= 9.
optionFeedback: This isn't stylistic — isSorted rest would silently skip a comparison. Try tracing isSorted [5,1,9] with isSorted rest to see it accept an unsorted list.
Correct — y is the head of the next comparison, so it has to be carried forward into the next call.
rest is a perfectly ordinary list on its own — the issue is which comparisons get made, not validity.
This is about correctness, not performance — both versions do the same amount of work, but only one checks every adjacent pair.

questions.question: In atPosition, two things shrink on the recursive call. What are they, and why does that matter?
options: Only y shrinks; the list stays the same size throughout
The list loses its head (xs is shorter than the original) and y decreases by 1 — both must reach their target together for the function to work
Only the list shrinks; y is unused
x and y both shrink, but the list itself never changes
questions.explanation: Each call moves to xs (one element shorter) and y - 1 (one smaller). They are kept in lockstep on purpose: when y reaches 0, the current head of the (now-shrunk) list is exactly the element originally at position y in the full list.
optionFeedback: The list argument shrinks too — atPosition (x:xs) y recurses on xs, not on the original list.
Correct — both xs and y shrink by one each call, and the correctness of the function depends on them staying synchronized.
y decreases on every call — it's what atPosition xs (y - 1) does, and it's essential: it's how the function knows when it has arrived at the target position.
The list argument does change — it becomes xs, one element shorter, on every recursive call.

questions.question: atPosition' uses xs !! y directly instead of recursing by hand. What must it check first, and why?
options: Nothing — !! already handles every case safely
y < 0 and y >= length xs, because !! is itself a partial function that crashes on an out-of-range index
Only that the list is non-empty
That y is even
questions.explanation: !! is partial, just like head — it throws Prelude.!!: index too large rather than failing gracefully. atPosition' guards against both a negative index and one at or beyond length xs before ever calling !!, producing a clearer error message instead of an unhandled exception.
optionFeedback: !! is one of the partial functions flagged in the previous lesson — it crashes on bad indices rather than handling them.
Correct — both guards exist specifically because !! itself does not check its index.
Checking non-emptiness alone isn't enough — a non-empty list can still have y far outside its valid index range.
There's no parity requirement on valid indices — even and odd positions are both perfectly normal.

questions.question: In evensUpTo, what determines when the recursion stops, given that there is no list to shrink toward []?
options: It never stops — evensUpTo would run forever
The counter k, once it exceeds n, matches the k > n guard and go returns [] with no further recursive call
It stops after exactly two recursive calls, always
It stops when k becomes negative
questions.explanation: There is no list argument shrinking here — the thing shrinking toward its base case is the gap between k and n. Once k > n, the guard fires, go returns [] directly, and the chain of pending conses can finally be built during rewinding.
optionFeedback: It does terminate, for exactly the reason a base case usually guarantees: k moves strictly closer to exceeding n on every call (k + 2 each time).
Correct — k > n plays the role [] plays in a consuming recursion: it is the condition that ends the recursive chain.
The number of calls depends entirely on n — evensUpTo 20 takes far more calls than evensUpTo 8.
k counts upward from 2 by 2s here; it is compared against n, not checked against 0 or negativity.

questions.question: Why does evensDown (which counts down from n, consing along the way) return [8,6,4,2] for evensDown 8, instead of the ascending [2,4,6,8]?
options: It doesn't — this is a typo, and evensDown 8 actually returns [2,4,6,8]
Because the first element consed on, during the earliest call, is 8 itself — and consing always places the new head at the front of whatever comes after it
Because even numbers are always listed in descending order in Haskell
Because evensDown has a bug unrelated to the direction it counts
questions.explanation: evensDown 8 = 8 : evensDown 7 = 8 : evensDown 6 = 8 : (6 : evensDown 5) = ... — 8 is consed on right away, at the very first call, so it ends up at the front of the whole result. Counting down and consing immediately builds the list in the order the counting happens, which is the reverse of counting up.
optionFeedback: This is exactly what evensDown 8 evaluates to — the CommonMistake box traces it by hand, and it really is backwards.
Correct — the earliest cons (of the largest survivor) ends up outermost, hence at the front, giving descending order.
There's nothing special about even numbers here; the same backwards-order issue would happen counting down through any values.
The direction it counts is exactly the cause — evensUpTo, which counts the other way, produces the correct ascending order with the same overall shape of definition.

check-constraint-vs-argument-in-a-signat.title: Check: constraint vs argument in a signature

questions.question: In linearSearch :: Eq a => [a] -> a -> Bool, how many arguments does linearSearch actually take?
options: Three — Eq a, [a], and a
Two — a list of a, and one a; Eq a => is a constraint on the type variable, not a third argument
One — the whole Eq a => [a] -> a part is a single combined argument
It depends on which type a is instantiated to
questions.explanation: Everything before => constrains what a is allowed to be; it is never itself a value you supply. Only the arrows after => separate actual arguments: [a] is the first, a is the second, and Bool is the result. linearSearch [1,2,3] 2 supplies exactly those two.
optionFeedback: Eq a is a constraint, not a value — there is no way to 'pass' Eq a as an argument the way you pass [1,2,3] or 2.
Correct — two ordinary arguments after the constraint, exactly as a call like linearSearch [1,2,3] 2 shows.
The constraint and the first argument type are separated by => precisely because they are different kinds of thing — a requirement on a type, versus the type of a real argument.
The number of arguments is fixed by the signature's arrow structure and never changes based on which concrete type a becomes.

questions.question: Once contains finds a match and returns True, what happens to the rest of the list that was not yet inspected?
options: It is still fully traversed before True is returned, just to be thorough
It is never inspected — the matching equation returns True immediately, with no further recursive call made
It causes a runtime error, since the list wasn't fully consumed
contains restarts from the beginning to double-check
questions.explanation: contains v (x:xs) | v == x = True fires as soon as the guard is True — the whole expression is just True, with no recursive call anywhere in that branch. Nothing after the matching element is ever looked at.
optionFeedback: There is nothing in the definition that forces the rest of the list to be visited — the True branch contains no call to contains at all.
Correct — the moment v == x holds, the answer is True and no further recursive call happens; the remaining tail is simply never inspected.
Returning early is completely normal and well-defined; it is not a partial pattern or an unhandled case.
contains has no notion of restarting; each call proceeds forward through the list exactly once, and stops the instant it can.

questions.question: What does positionOf 100 [3,7,9,2] return, and why?
options: 4, the length of the list, as if 100 were appended at the end
-1, because 100 never matches any element and go eventually reaches [] with i = 4
An error, since 100 is not in the list
0, defaulting to the first position
questions.explanation: go checks each element in turn, incrementing i each time none matches: i reaches 0, 1, 2, 3 across the four elements, none of which is 100, and then go [] 4 hits the base case, returning -1 regardless of what i had counted up to.
optionFeedback: The base case go [] _ = -1 discards i entirely — the running count is not what gets returned when nothing matches.
Correct — positionOf is total for this case: it does not crash, it reports -1 as its 'not found' sentinel.
positionOf never calls error; -1 is its designed way of reporting absence, matching the Bool version's False.
0 would mean the first element matched, which it doesn't here — none of the four elements is 100.

deeper-reasoning-structural-recursion-on.title: Deeper reasoning: structural recursion on lists

questions.question: A student writes doubleAll without the [] equation, because "the question never mentions an empty list". The file loads without errors and the student is confident. Which assessment of what happens when doubleAll [1, 2, 3] is run is the most accurate?
options: It prints [2,4,6], because Haskell treats the missing [] case as returning [] by default.

It stops with a non-exhaustive patterns exception. The recursion removes one element per call, so after three steps it reaches [], which no equation matches. The [] equation is what stops the recursion, so it is needed even when the problem statement says nothing about empty lists. GHC accepts the file because incomplete patterns are not an error by default, which is why -Wincomplete-patterns is worth switching on.
It never finishes, because without a base case the recursion carries on forever with longer and longer lists.
It does not compile, because every recursive function must contain the empty list pattern.
questions.explanation: Every list recursion ends at the empty list, so the base case is part of the algorithm and not an optional extra. The list gets shorter on each call, so the recursion terminates, but in a crash rather than a result.
optionFeedback: Haskell never supplies a missing equation. If nothing matches, the call fails.
Correct. The argument shrinks as required, but the end of the list is a case that must be handled.
The list gets shorter, not longer, so the recursion does end. It ends with an exception.
GHC accepts incomplete patterns by default, so the file compiles. The failure appears when the missing case is reached.

questions.question: A student writes largerY to keep the elements larger than y. Running largerY [7, 3, 10] 4 gives [7] instead of [7,10]. Which analysis identifies the fault and the general rule it breaks?
code: | x > y     = x : largerY xs y
options: The fault is the first guard: x : largerY xs y should be largerY xs y so that the head is not duplicated.
The fault is the base case, which should return the original list instead of [].

When an element fails the test, the skipping branch must still recurse on the tail, as in largerY xs y. Returning [] there ends the whole result at the first rejected element, so everything after 3 is lost, including 10. In a filter, both branches recurse on xs; only the kept branch conses the head onto the result.
The function is correct, and the expected answer for the classmate's input is [7].
questions.explanation: The structure of a recursive filter has two branches that differ in one detail: whether the head is consed on. Both branches continue with the tail. A branch that returns [] turns a filter into a take-while.
optionFeedback: The kept branch is correct: it conses the head onto the filtered tail. Removing the cons would drop the elements that should be kept.
The empty list is the correct base case. Returning the original list would keep elements that should be filtered out.
Correct. The hand trace of [7, 3, 10] shows the result being cut off at 3.
The specification keeps every element larger than y, so 10 belongs in the result.

questions.question: A student implements isSorted with only two equations, reasoning that the one-element case is "obviously sorted and does not need its own line". Their test isSorted [3, 1, 5] returns False as expected, so they submit it. Which analysis predicts what actually happens for a genuinely sorted input such as [5, 3, 1]?
options: isSorted [5, 3, 1] returns True, because the recursion ends at the empty list.
isSorted [5, 3, 1] returns False, because a single element is treated as unsorted.

isSorted [5, 3, 1] crashes. The recursion passes through isSorted [3, 1] and then isSorted [1], and the list [1] has one element, which matches neither [] nor (x:y:rest). A sorted input is exactly the kind that reaches the one-element case, whereas an unsorted input such as [3, 1, 5] stops early with False and never gets there. The test chosen could not reveal the gap, and the missing equation isSorted [_] = True is required.
isSorted [5, 3, 1] crashes only if the list contains a negative number.
questions.explanation: A pattern that looks at two elements at a time needs a case for lists that are too short, and the recursion shrinks its input by one each time, so it will always arrive there on a sorted list. Testing only an unsorted input hides the crash.
optionFeedback: The list never becomes empty on this path: the recursion removes one element at a time and stops at a list with one element.
Haskell does not treat the one-element list specially. With no matching equation, the call fails.
Correct. The failing path is only exercised by sorted inputs, so a test set should include both sorted and unsorted lists, and lists of length 0, 1 and 2.
The values in the list make no difference to which equation is chosen. The shape of the list does.
